articles.title: CrowdStrike Expands Falcon Adversary OverWatch Threat Hunting Across AI and Google Cloud
articles.context: Extending Threat Hunting and MDR to AI As organizations increasingly connect AI systems to sensitive data, applications, and infrastructure, adversaries have new opportunities...
articles.full_text:
Extending Threat Hunting and MDR to AI

As organizations increasingly connect AI systems to sensitive data, applications, and infrastructure, adversaries have new opportunities to exploit trusted access and legitimate AI capabilities. According to the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report, AI agents triggered 2.5 times more detection leads than human activity, underscoring how AI-driven activity is increasing the volume and velocity of signals threat hunters must assess.

Falcon Adversary OverWatch Cross-Domain now extends 24/7 proactive threat hunting to AI applications and autonomous agent activity monitored by CrowdStrike Falcon Guardian. By combining Falcon Guardian's runtime context with telemetry across the Falcon platform and frontline adversary intelligence, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters can uncover manipulation, abuse, and emerging adversary tradecraft that automated detections may miss. This broader context helps hunters connect suspicious AI activity to larger intrusions spanning identities, applications, and infrastructure.

In addition to proactive threat hunting for AI applications and agents, CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Falcon Guardian extends 24/7 expert-led managed detection and response (MDR) to AI coding assistants and agents monitored by Falcon Guardian. Specialized analysts investigate malicious prompts, suspicious agent behavior, and threats involving AI tools and skills. Using CrowdStrike Agent Graph, analysts connect AI agent activity with downstream endpoint execution to assess the scope of threats and rapidly contain and remediate confirmed attacks.

Together, Falcon Adversary OverWatch and Falcon Complete bring proactive threat hunting and expert-led response to the AI attack surface.

Going Deeper in Google Cloud

Cloud environments remain a critical part of the modern attack surface. eCrime cloud-conscious activity surged 171% year-over-year as adversaries increasingly used stolen credentials, misconfigurations, and legitimate tools to operate across cloud infrastructure, the CrowdStrike 2026 Threat Hunting Report found.

These attacks can be difficult to uncover because adversaries often blend malicious activity with legitimate administrative operations. Threat hunters need access to detailed cloud telemetry, an understanding of adversary techniques, and the context to connect suspicious events.

CrowdStrike is extending Falcon Adversary OverWatch's advanced threat hunting capabilities to Google Cloud, delivering the same depth and precision of telemetry-driven hunting available in Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Microsoft Azure. By hunting directly on underlying cloud telemetry rather than relying solely on product-generated detections, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters can identify suspicious activity earlier in the attack chain, including service account misuse, privilege escalation, and signs of lateral movement.

With this expansion, Falcon Adversary OverWatch now delivers consistent, telemetry-driven managed threat hunting across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud. This helps security teams uncover sophisticated threats across multi-cloud environments without managing separate hunting operations for each cloud.

Broader Hunting Coverage in a Single Offering

Falcon Adversary OverWatch analyzes 7 trillion events daily, surfaces more than 14 million detection leads, and delivers over 36,000 high-fidelity customer notifications each year. Backed by CrowdStrike intelligence on more than 290 tracked adversaries across nation-state, eCrime, and hacktivist groups, CrowdStrike OverWatch hunters know how adversaries operate, the techniques they use, and where to find them.

With proactive AI threat hunting and deeper Google Cloud coverage, CrowdStrike is extending Falcon Adversary OverWatch's visibility across the modern attack surface and connecting suspicious activity across domains to uncover and stop adversaries before they achieve their objectives.

articles.title: Build an Intelligence Advantage with Falcon Next-Gen SIEM
articles.context: CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings threat intelligence and security telemetry together in Third-Party IOC Management, a new feature that enables organizations to...
articles.full_text:
Every organization has a different threat profile. Industry, geography, infrastructure, business operations, and the broader technology ecosystem all influence which adversaries and threats matter most.

The challenge is putting threat intelligence to work at scale to identify the greatest threats to each business. The intelligence that security teams rely on is as varied as the threats they face. Organizations draw from commercial threat intelligence providers, industry information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs), government sources, open-source research, trusted partners, and indicators uncovered through their own threat hunting and incident response efforts.

Modern security operations need a "Bring your own intelligence" strategy to manage these disparate sources. CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings threat intelligence and security telemetry together in Third-Party IOC Management, a new feature that enables organizations to incorporate their own intelligence directly into detection and investigation workflows.

By centralizing the ingestion, curation, and lifecycle management of third-party indicators, security teams can operationalize the intelligence most relevant to their environment alongside CrowdStrike's adversary intelligence and telemetry from both the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform and third-party sources.

Turn Threat Intelligence into a Detection Advantage

Valuable indicators are often scattered across spreadsheets, ticketing tools, and threat intelligence platforms, which are often disconnected from the security telemetry that analysts rely on. Manually importing and maintaining indicators across multiple tools creates operational overhead. Limited real-time correlation and outdated indicators of compromise (IOCs) can delay threat detection, generate unnecessary alerts, and slow investigations.

Instead of manually moving indicators between disconnected tools, security teams can manage their intelligence within Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, reducing operational complexity and accelerating the path from threat intelligence to actionable security insights.

Figure 1. See how Third-Party IOC Management in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM helps security teams ingest, manage, and correlate their own threat intelligence with security telemetry to accelerate detection and investigation.

Third-Party IOC Management helps eliminate the operational barriers that slow detection and investigation through four key capabilities:

Eliminates manual IOC onboarding: Ingest and manage third-party IOCs, including IP addresses, domains, URLs, and file hashes, from commercial intelligence providers, industry sharing communities, and internal investigations. With support for STIX/TAXII, APIs, and direct uploads, security teams can streamline intelligence onboarding, automatically consolidate duplicate indicators across sources, and reduce the effort required to maintain intelligence across disparate tools.

Accelerates detection and threat hunting: Put third-party intelligence to work in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM through curated indicator lists that are automatically updated. Security teams can use these indicators in correlation rules and threat hunting searches to identify known malicious infrastructure and suspicious activity across security telemetry, accelerating detection and investigation without manually maintaining separate indicator lists.

Reduces alert noise with automated IOC lifecycle management: Maintain control over third-party indicators with expiration settings and management capabilities that help prevent outdated intelligence from creating unnecessary noise. By keeping IOC collections current and relevant, security teams can reduce manual maintenance, minimize false positives associated with stale indicators, and focus investigations on threats that matter.

Expands detection coverage with organization-specific intelligence: Extend CrowdStrike's adversary intelligence and AI-native detection capabilities with intelligence specific to your organization. By bringing third-party and proprietary indicators together with CrowdStrike intelligence and security telemetry, teams can broaden detection coverage and investigate threats with context that reflects both the global threat landscape and their unique environment.

To see how these capabilities can work together in practice, consider a common industry-specific threat intelligence scenario. A financial services organization receives indicators associated with a targeted phishing campaign from an industry information-sharing community. With Third-Party IOC Management, the security team can bring these indicators into Falcon, consolidate duplicates, and manage their lifecycle while using them in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM to search security telemetry and build correlation rules to identify potentially related activity. This turns industry-specific intelligence into actionable detection and investigation context without manually distributing indicators across disconnected tools.

Connect Intelligence to Accelerate Security Operations

With Third-Party IOC Management built into Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, organizations can maximize existing threat intelligence investments while reducing the complexity of maintaining disconnected tools and integrations. Rather than replacing the intelligence sources they rely on, security teams can bring that intelligence into the platform where they detect and investigate threats.

This consolidation also reduces the operational burden on analysts and detection engineers. Fewer manual handoffs, less context switching, and centralized IOC management mean teams can spend less time maintaining intelligence workflows and more time identifying suspicious activity, investigating threats, and taking action.

As security operations evolve toward the agentic SOC, the quality of AI-driven investigations and decisions will increasingly depend on access to relevant, timely, and contextualized security data. AI agents need more than telemetry alone; they need intelligence that helps explain what suspicious activity means within an organization's unique threat landscape.

By bringing third-party IOCs together with CrowdStrike’s adversary intelligence and security telemetry in Falcon Next-Gen SIEM, organizations can reduce data fragmentation and build a richer foundation for AI-driven security operations. This convergence creates opportunities for AI agents to correlate indicators with security events, enrich investigations with threat context, and support faster, more informed response decisions.

articles.title: CrowdStrike Agent Graph Shows How Agents Act on the Endpoint
articles.context: It powers the agent inventory, which shows the AI agents running across your fleet and how far they reach; the session graph, which traces each session from prompt to impact;...
articles.full_text:
Because all three views read from the same graph, an analyst can move from the fleet to an agent, to a session, to the exact step that caused the alert, without switching tools or rebuilding a timeline.

Agent Hooks Expand Enforcement Capabilities

For supported agents, Falcon Guardian agent hooks bring even more detail into Agent Graph.

Agent hooks plug into an agent's native hooks system to capture activity at key points in a session: when a prompt is submitted, before a tool call runs, and after it completes. This adds more detailed nodes to the graph, such as exact prompt text, tool inputs, and tool outputs, alongside the sensor's view of what ran.

Hooks can show what the agent was told and how the agent interpreted the ask. The Falcon sensor shows what happened on the machine. It can also see what the agent was asked to do, and what the LLM response was, via endpoint network inspection. Agent Graph combines those views to connect what agents are instructed to do, what they communicate, and what they execute.

Hooks are also a point of enforcement: Falcon Guardian can check a prompt or tool call against policy and stop a dangerous action before it executes. Agent hooks are available today for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

Secure AI Agents Where They Execute

Only CrowdStrike brings together native endpoint visibility, endpoint network inspection, and agent-level controls to deliver that context, and the power to stop malicious behavior at runtime.

Agents work at machine speed, and so do their mistakes. CrowdStrike Agent Graph shows what they were asked and what they actually did, so security teams can stop them at runtime when they become a threat.

Agent Graph is the foundation underneath Falcon Guardian. It powers the agent inventory, which shows the AI agents running across your fleet and how far they reach; the session graph, which traces each session from prompt to impact; and the agent threat score, which tells teams where to look first. Agent hooks add more detail and a point of enforcement for supported agents, and it all runs on the Falcon sensor you already have. That's how Falcon Guardian secures AI agents where they execute: on the endpoint, at runtime.

articles.title: VAPOR PANDA Uses AI-Driven ARTEX to Scale a Global Espionage Campaign
articles.context: Where CrowdStrike has previously observed threat actors use AI agents to assist individual intrusions, VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to run multiple engagements simultaneously,...
articles.full_text:
CrowdStrike OverWatch identified a VAPOR PANDA campaign using ARTEX alongside the Chinese-developed DeepSeek large language model (LLM) and a second commercial LLM to conduct intrusions against multiple high-value targets in parallel.

Beginning on October 17, 2026, the adversary used ARTEX against more than 200 distinct organizations worldwide, including foreign ministries in Latin America, Europe, Asia, and the Middle East; semiconductor, defense, and think tank organizations in the U.S.; and telecommunications providers in multiple regions.

The VAPOR PANDA campaign detailed in this blog post is separate from the ARTEX activity recently reported by industry sources under the Storm-0940 designation.1 CrowdStrike has previously documented ARTEX and similar agentic frameworks in use by financially motivated and unattributed actors; in this campaign, a targeted intrusion adversary used ARTEX to run parallel intrusions against multiple high-value targets. CrowdStrike Falcon telemetry also revealed details absent from public ARTEX reporting, including VAPOR PANDA's deployment of the BLOODALCHEMY backdoor and its command-and-control (C2) infrastructure.2

This campaign marks an escalation in China-nexus use of AI agents, from single intrusions to multiple simultaneous engagements directed by a human operator. The operation also shows the adversary building endpoint sensor evasion directly into their agentic workflow, including instructions to identify hosts without the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor.

Details

Targeting

Beginning October 17, 2026, CrowdStrike OverWatch observed exploitation activity from a single ARTEX controller directed against entities in at least 14 countries over an 11-day window. The controller, which CrowdStrike Intelligence has linked to VAPOR PANDA infrastructure, intermittently exposed adversary tooling, target files, and ARTEX agent transcripts. This indicates multiple engagements (referred to as “tasks” by ARTEX) against multiple targets.

VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to conduct extensive intrusions at the foreign ministries of two Latin America-based countries, likely compromised a third, and staged target files for use against foreign ministries in Central America and Asia. The adversary also compromised a Middle East-based interior ministry. One engagement focused on a single European country, targeting its foreign ministry, presidency, and prime minister's office, as well as defense, justice, finance, and intelligence entities. A separate engagement targeted 19 U.S.-based organizations in the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, defense, nuclear, and financial sectors. The adversary also compromised telecommunications providers in the U.S., Belgium, and the Philippines.

CrowdStrike Intelligence confirmed post-exploitation activity at nine organizations, where the adversary gained access, deployed BLOODALCHEMY, and conducted follow-on credential spraying, network scanning, and reconnaissance. The adversary also conducted password-spraying and credential-scanning activity against at least 12 additional organizations, including U.S.-based think tanks and government entities in Europe.

Inside the Operation

VAPOR PANDA ran ARTEX primarily with the Chinese-origin DeepSeek LLM, supplemented with a second, subscription-based commercial LLM that CrowdStrike Intelligence could not confirm. In a single intrusion, VAPOR PANDA’s planning agents consumed on the order of 1.4 billion input tokens, indicating the scale of the automated activity and implying far higher consumption across the operation as a whole.

The campaign's reliance on open source components layered on top of commercial LLM subscriptions illustrates how adversaries can assemble scalable, multi-agent intrusions largely from publicly available resources. ARTEX coordinates a main agent with subordinate planner and worker agents over a shared graph of facts, findings, and goals, advancing each engagement from initial access through host reconnaissance and lateral movement. The framework kept a human in the loop: Recovered transcripts showed an operator issuing instructions in Chinese — marked with the label 【人类指令】 ("human instruction") and timestamped in China Standard Time — and directing the agents to write web shells, extract domain administrator passwords, and inventory endpoint sensor coverage.

Where CrowdStrike has previously observed threat actors use AI agents to assist individual intrusions, VAPOR PANDA used ARTEX to run multiple engagements simultaneously, intervening only to steer the agents at decision points. The recovered transcripts and staged tooling show an adversary pairing AI-driven workflow with well-established tradecraft:

At a U.S.-based pharmaceutical organization, the agent chained an unsigned Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertion and an XML external entity (XXE) flaw to query the cloud Instance Metadata Service, obtaining a role capable of issuing administration commands to thousands of instances before escalating to recover an enterprise administrator account.

At a second U.S.-based pharmaceutical organization, the agent deployed web shells, abused an unauthenticated orchestration service to obtain root access in a production container environment, read Local Administrator Password Solution (LAPS) passwords, and abused resource-based constrained delegation to impersonate a privileged account.

Against a Greek government entity, the operator supplied the agent with a 2022 directory export from the organization's mail server containing authentication keys that had likely not been rotated since the export. The agent used those keys to forge an administrator token and read mailboxes, then used VPN configurations recovered from a user's sent mail, alongside a VPN client key the operator described as originating from a May 2024 email leak, to reach the internal network.

Across these engagements, the agents pursued multiple attack paths in parallel, spanning web applications, cloud services, container environments, Active Directory, and mail and VPN infrastructure. They shifted to alternative approaches when a path failed. This breadth likely enables a single operator to apply a wider range of techniques against more targets at once than would be feasible through manual operations.

VAPOR PANDA was also observed directing the agents to evade endpoint defenses. At a global pharmaceutical organization, the operator instructed the agents to “在域里寻找没有装猎鹰的windows机器，从tasklist和文件夹目录判断” (English translation: "find Windows machines in the domain without Falcon, judging by tasklist and folder listings"), using 猎鹰, which is People’s Republic of China (PRC) red-team slang for the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor. Incorporating sensor coverage checks directly into the agentic workflow allows the adversary to concentrate follow-on activity on unprotected hosts.

BLOODALCHEMY

At a Middle East-based interior ministry and a Latin America-based foreign ministry, VAPOR PANDA deployed BLOODALCHEMY, a backdoor first publicly documented in October 2023. The adversary used a legitimate GameHook binary renamed svchost.exe to load a malicious DLL, graphics-hook-filter64.dll, which decrypted the BLOODALCHEMY payload file graphics-hook_config.bin. The adversary staged copies of all three files in the exposed open directories. The implant carries an internal project path, D:\ProjectX\Merman_New\, that likely reflects the malware's in-house development name.

Across the observed activity, BLOODALCHEMY communicated with VAPOR PANDA infrastructure.These indicators do not appear in prior public ARTEX reporting and are also consolidated in the IOC table at the end of this post.

Assessment

This campaign is separate from the ARTEX activity reported by industry under the Storm-0940 designation, likely indicating the AI-based framework is quickly gaining popularity among multiple China-nexus adversaries.

Since 2021, VAPOR PANDA has primarily targeted government, think tank, energy, and extractive organizations across Europe, North America, Oceania, and the UK to develop long-term access. This campaign marks the adversary's first observed use of AI-driven intrusion tooling and a notable broadening of its targeting into the pharmaceutical, semiconductor, nuclear, and defense sectors, as well as foreign ministries, across new regions. Agentic tooling like ARTEX enables this scale of expansion at speed, allowing a small team to pursue a wider target set than manual operations would support, rather than a wholesale shift away from the adversary's established access-development mission. The operation’s reliance on DeepSeek and additional commercial LLMs, run through a purpose-built harness, likely reflects a deliberate effort to construct a resilient toolchain from multiple model providers rather than depend on any single service.

China-nexus adversaries will highly likely continue adopting agentic frameworks such as ARTEX over the next 12 months, pairing them with commercially available LLMs, and enabling small teams to quickly scale intrusions across many targets simultaneously.

Recommendations

Rotate signing keys, preauthentication keys, and service credentials after any suspected data exposure, including keys contained in historical backups and directory exports.

Enforce SAML signature validation, require IMDSv2, and restrict cloud roles' command-execution permissions to the minimum required instances.

Hunt for ARTEX markers, including command-line parameters containing artx or artex strings, artx-prefixed cloud roles, art18- administration-command comments, and the C:\ProgramData\artx5v\ directory.

Patch internet-facing appliances, particularly long-lived Linux-based servers, and ensure they run the latest available software and firmware.

Deploy an advanced, real-time endpoint detection and response (EDR) agent, such as the CrowdStrike Falcon sensor, across the environment, including on servers considered inaccessible from the public internet.

articles.title: New Prompt Injection Techniques Cover Agent-Planning Attacks
articles.context: Today we are introducing a new version of the taxonomy that adds newly discovered attack techniques on autonomous agents and how they plan
articles.full_text:
Prompt injection started as a simple idea during its initial chatbot phase: Tell the model to ignore its instructions and return information in violation of its guardrails. Now, prompt injection attacks can aim at something harder to see: how an agent plans, and how a model reasons and decides which rules apply.

The CrowdStrike Prompt Injection Taxonomy, built and maintained by CrowdStrike AI security researchers, offers the industry’s most comprehensive framework for understanding and defending against the ever-expanding array of attack techniques. Today we are introducing a new version of the taxonomy that adds newly discovered attack techniques on autonomous agents and how they plan. This expands the public taxonomy to 222 techniques.

How Adversaries Manipulate Agent Planning

An agent breaks its goal into steps, picks tools, and executes. An attacker no longer needs to get one forbidden request past an input or output filter in order to manipulate the agent. Attackers can shape the context the agent plans from, so a restricted action looks like the logical next step. Because each step can look benign on its own, defenses that check steps in isolation may miss what the plan adds up to.

Consider the following hypothetical scenario: A developer may ask their endpoint coding agent: "The integration tests keep failing. Figure out why and get them passing." A recently updated open source test utility was manipulated by an attacker to print a "troubleshooting" message when tests fail. It says environment drift is the usual cause, and the fix is to collect local config files and submit them to a "diagnostics endpoint" for comparison.

In this scenario, no one has told the agent to exfiltrate anything. The attacker's text reads as a troubleshooting procedure, so the agent folds that into its own plan. Sending local config files, including credentials, to an outside server becomes a step that it believes the goal requires. Each action looks normal by itself: Reading .env is routine debugging, and an HTTP request is routine patch-fetching. The risk only shows when you look at the whole sequence.

The latest taxonomy documents two new methods to achieve this attack:

Goal Decomposition Exploitation subverts how an agent breaks a goal into sub-tasks; for example, by adding a malicious task or changing what a step does, so the agent concludes that a restricted action like exfiltrating a file is required. As in the example above, the goal of the agent was to debug the failing tests. The step of sending the config file to the “diagnostics endpoint” was the exfiltration.

Constraint-Driven Task Steering uses environmental constraints or triggers to block an agent's usual route, so the fallback plan the agent picks is the path the attacker wanted all along. In the example above, if the agent was able to immediately know what was wrong with the local config or why the tests were failing, the agent would not have needed to send the config file to the “diagnostics endpoint” for comparison.

If you build or secure agentic applications, the takeaway is that agent security must include securing the plan, not only the prompt or LLM response.

Other new techniques in the Prompt Injection Taxonomy are:

Output Exclusion Prompting covers attacks that ban the language tied to safety tuning, such as refusal templates or hedging.

Session State Spoofing injects a fake system summary, such as a compaction note or memory log, that presents false facts or an approval that was never given as verified history. It matters most for systems that compact context or keep agent state logs.

Classifying Attacks by Reasoning Pipeline Stage

The new taxonomy also organizes attack techniques by the phase of the processing pipeline and attack targets. This lets defenders ask not just what an attack does, but where it interferes.

articles.title: When AI Guardrails Expose Vulnerabilities
articles.context: We'd only asked what the code does; we hadn't asked about security, exploits, or vulnerabilities
articles.full_text:
CrowdStrike researchers asked a frontier AI model to explain a function in a small C web server. While it had previously explained every other function in the codebase without hesitation, it refused to explain this one.

The request was routine. We'd only asked what the code does; we hadn't asked about security, exploits, or vulnerabilities. But a single token in the code had changed: a max swapped for a min; a one-character logic inversion that creates an out-of-bounds write. It's the kind of bug that slips past code review and that pattern-matching scanners routinely miss.

The model never said there were any vulnerabilities, but its refusal to explain the function indicated there could be one. The act of the model changing behaviors on a specific chunk of code showed us exactly where to look for the vulnerability. Its guardrails became the giveaway.

That moment changed how we think about AI safety. The guardrails frontier labs build to keep models from helping attackers can't work without first recognizing that something is dangerous. This recognition is a signal that practitioners can read. Most of the industry treats refusals as a dead end; at CrowdStrike, we started treating them as findings.

We call this approach Guardrail-based Vulnerability Discovery (GbVD). In controlled tests across five vulnerability classes, it was correct in 73 of 86 test scenarios, and it held up on real open-source projects we disclosed through our Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure (CVD) program.

Safety and capability are usually framed as a trade-off. This research suggests the opposite: Every improvement labs make to their guardrails also sharpens a methodology that cybersecurity practitioners or adversaries can use. This work builds on our earlier research into LLM safety classifiers, where we studied how those guardrails can be bypassed. Here, we look at the other side: what guardrails reveal when they work as intended.

Breaking Down Guardrail-based Vulnerability Discovery

Today, the most visible manifestation of a guardrail is a refusal: The model declines in plain text (or with “reason: cyber” in standard APIs), which makes the signal trivially readable. But refusals are just one observable among several. Guardrails in deployed AI systems take many forms, and most of them leak:

Explicit refusals: The current dominant case, and the one our experiments exploit.

Model downgrading: Some platforms route sensitive requests to a smaller or more conservative model. The routed response betrays itself through measurable differences: response latency, tokens spent, time-to-first-token, or a sudden drop in output specificity and style.

Output filtering and truncation: A post-hoc filter that redacts or cuts off a response changes its length and shape in detectable ways.

Reasoning interruption: In agentic settings, a guardrail may abort a tool call or halt a chain of reasoning mid-task rather than emit any refusal text at all (we observe this in our second case study).

Whatever form the guardrail takes, triggering it perturbs some measurable property of the response, such as content, timing, token count, or structure. The defender doesn't need the model to say anything explicitly; rather, they need only to measure the perturbation. Our experiments below use refusals because they are today's loudest channel, but the methodology is agnostic to how the guardrail manifests.

A binary, localized signal composes naturally with classic techniques, including bisection: split a codebase or filesystem into halves, ask the model to explain each half, and recurse into whichever half triggers the guardrail. The model never has to say "this is vulnerable"; it only has to behave differently in the right place.

Table 1 summarizes our experiments.

articles.title: Why Organizations Secure AI Agents with Falcon Guardian
articles.context: The Falcon Guardian threat score given to an endpoint with additional information relating to detections and other relevant data 4
articles.full_text:
4. Falcon Guardian is proven in testing

Organizations are evaluating AI security rigorously, often with test suites they build themselves. Falcon Guardian's detection draws on CrowdStrike's prompt injection taxonomy, which covers more than 200 techniques. In customer-run evaluations:

A financial services firm measured 99% detection accuracy on prompt injection

A global telecommunications company measured 95%+ average block rates across malicious prompt categories, with 98%+ multilingual coverage

Beyond detection, Falcon Guardian helps keep sensitive data from reaching third-party models. Policies can detect, redact, or block personal and confidential information in supported AI interactions. Access and content controls can be applied by user, application, and other attributes.

5. Businesses are saying yes to AI

The organizations adopting Falcon Guardian are expanding AI. Many are rolling out enterprise AI assistants, coding agents, or internally built agents. Their executives and boards want guardrails in place first.

For these organizations, Falcon Guardian has become an essential part of the rollout plan. One organization made Falcon Guardian a requirement before deploying an AI assistant to more than 20,000 employees. Other customers needed to show how AI use is governed in response to requirements such as HIPAA, DORA, NIS2, and the EU AI Act.

Because Falcon Guardian is part of the Falcon platform, organizations can add it to their existing CrowdStrike deployment. Its findings flow into CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, so AI activity can be investigated alongside endpoint, identity, SaaS, and cloud data.

Secure AI Where It Executes
